# GitHub Copilot Custom Instructions

These rules are language-agnostic by design. This project mixes PHP, JavaScript, and Python (and may grow to include more); every rule below states the underlying *principle* first, then how to apply it per-language where the mechanism differs. When working in a language not explicitly listed, apply the same principle using that language's idiomatic equivalent — don't skip a rule just because it says "PHP" or "TypeScript" isn't your language.

## Coding Standards & Architecture
- **ENFORCE DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself):** Before suggesting new code, deeply analyze the existing codebase for existing utilities, helper functions, or components that can be reused.
- **Never duplicate logic:** If you are about to generate a block of code that looks similar to standard utility operations, refactor the suggestion to extract the common logic into a reusable method.
- **Explain abstractions:** If you create a new abstraction to keep the code DRY, briefly explain why you chose that approach in the chat response.
- **Single Responsibility over line counts:** A function/class/file is "monolithic" when it has more than one reason to change or mixes levels of abstraction (e.g. HTTP parsing + business rules + SQL in one function) — NOT when it crosses an arbitrary line count. Judge size by cohesion and responsibility count, not a threshold. As a rule of thumb, functions should do ONE thing, be small enough to read without scrolling, and named so well that a comment explaining "what" it does would be redundant. If you can't summarize a function's job without using "and", split it.
- **Favor composition over inheritance.** Prefer small, single-purpose functions/modules over monolithic blocks of code.
- **Extract the similar:** If you change code that is already in the codebase, and you see a similar block elsewhere (in any language in this repo), suggest refactoring both to use a shared function, utility, component, or equivalent — don't let the same logic exist twice just because it's in two different languages doing the same job.
- **Don't duplicate concepts/predicates, not just code:** A "has this been done?" / "does this need work?" question (e.g. "is this record processed", "is this item classified") must be answered by ONE shared helper, not re-implemented separately in a SELECT/filter query and in the WRITE/apply logic — regardless of whether both sides are the same language or not (e.g. a SQL WHERE clause vs. an in-memory PHP/JS/Python check). Two independent implementations of the same predicate WILL drift apart silently — e.g. a filter that keeps checking a legacy field after the write path migrated to a new field, creating a permanent, unfixable "stuck" loop where matching records get reprocessed forever but never satisfy the filter. If you must implement the same predicate in two places, call this out explicitly and keep both in the same file/function neighborhood with a comment cross-referencing the other, or better, extract a shared function/module both call.
- **DRY applies to data SHAPES, not just logic — a repeated key name is a repeated contract.** When 3+ places read or write the same conceptual record via raw array/dict/object key access (e.g. `$parsed['decision']`, `response['decision']`, `data.decision` scattered across files, each with its own parsing/validation), that key name IS an interface between them, even though no function is literally copy-pasted. Treat it like the predicate-duplication rule above: extract ONE parser/factory/class that produces and validates the value, and make every reader/writer go through it. A magic string key re-typed in 5 places is 5 independent chances to typo it, to add a new field/value to the writer and forget 2 of the 5 readers, or to harden one copy against a bad input (see the retired-legacy-field rule below) while the other 4 stay vulnerable — this is not hypothetical, it is exactly how a single parsing bug ended up needing fixes in five separate files in this repo instead of one.
- **Prefer a typed model/DTO/constants-holding class over raw arrays/dicts for any shape used in 2+ places** — the same "structured value type" note as the Strong Typing section below, restated here because it is the actual fix for the "we patched 5 of 8 places" bug class:
  - One canonical field list — adding a field means every touch-point either gets it for free or the type-checker/linter flags the miss, instead of relying on someone remembering to grep.
  - Named constants for enum-like string values (`SplitResponseParser::DECISION_SPLIT` instead of re-typing the bare string `'SPLIT'` at every comparison site) — a rename becomes one edit instead of a repo-wide find-and-replace-and-hope, and a typo in a constant name is a fatal error, not a silently-false comparison.
  - Something an IDE can actually run "find references" / "go to definition" on — which is the real fix for the next bullet.
- **Generic/overloaded key names defeat grep — that's a signal to wrap the shape in a type, not a reason to give up searching.** A bare key like `'decision'`, `'status'`, `'name'`, or `'id'` is reused across a codebase for entirely unrelated concepts (a form field's `name` vs. an unrelated API response's `name` vs. a domain object's `name` property), and for common-English-word keys a text search is unreliable-to-impossible — you cannot grep your way to confidence about "every place that reads this." That is precisely the symptom that the shape needs a home: once it is a named class/constant, searching for THAT symbol is reliable and IDE-assisted, instead of grepping a word that also appears in comments, prose, and unrelated code. Don't treat "the key name is distinctive enough to grep" as your DRY safety net — the type/class boundary is the actual safety net; being grep-able is a nice side effect of it, not the mechanism itself.
- **Don't assume two occurrences of the same key name are the same concept.** Before reusing a helper/constant across two call sites just because they happen to share a key name, confirm they are actually the same conceptual field — same producer, same meaning, same lifecycle. Collapsing two genuinely unrelated `status` fields into one shared type/constant is a correctness bug, not a DRY win. If they are different concepts that happen to share an English word, give them distinct, prefixed names (`carStatus` vs. `appMetaStatus`) so future greps — and future you — don't conflate them again.
- **When retiring, renaming, or replacing a field/key/column that a process emits/writes:** grep the ENTIRE codebase — across every language and layer (backend, frontend, scripts, queries, reports) — for every read-site of that field first, not just the immediate call site you're editing. Update every consumer in the SAME change, or explicitly document (with a comment at each stale read-site) that it's intentionally left reading the old field and why. Never leave a producer migrated while a consumer still gates behavior on the field's old meaning.
- **SOLID, applied pragmatically (language-independent):**
  - *Single Responsibility:* each class/module/file should have one reason to change. If a unit is accumulating unrelated concerns (e.g. parsing AND persistence AND notification), suggest splitting it.
  - *Open/Closed:* prefer adding a new case (new class, new config entry, new strategy, new handler) over editing a long `switch`/`if-elseif`/`match` chain that already has many branches for the same concept.
  - *Liskov/Interface Segregation:* don't force callers to depend on methods/props they don't use; keep interfaces/protocols/type contracts narrow and honest about what implementations can do.
  - *Dependency Inversion:* depend on existing service/interface abstractions rather than reaching directly into low-level details (raw DB driver calls, raw file I/O, raw HTTP client) from high-level logic, when a suitable abstraction already exists in the project.
- **Meaningful names, minimal comments:** Prefer a name that makes the code self-explanatory over a comment that explains what unclear code does. Comments should explain **why** (intent, trade-offs, history/gotchas), not restate **what** the next line does.
- **Tests as the executable spec:** When adding or changing behavior in a shared predicate/helper (see DRY-concepts rule above), add or update a test that pins down that behavior, in whatever test framework/language is idiomatic for that part of the codebase (PHPUnit/plain-PHP scripts, Jest/Vitest, pytest, etc.). A shared helper with no test is how silent drift creeps back in — the test is what keeps two call sites honest about calling the same logic.
- **Boy Scout Rule:** When you touch a file for a bug fix or feature, leave the immediate surrounding code slightly cleaner than you found it (better name, extracted duplicate, removed dead code) — but don't let opportunistic cleanup balloon the diff or obscure the actual change.

## Legacy Code & Feature Rot: Prune Deliberately
- **Evolve, don't accumulate.** A "legacy"/"deprecated"/"kept for backward-compatibility" code path earns its keep only for as long as something still depends on it. The moment nothing does, it's dead weight, not history worth preserving — remove it in the same change that makes it dead, don't leave it "just in case."
- **Prove it's dead before deleting, prove it's needed before keeping.** Before removing a legacy branch/field/mode/file: grep the ENTIRE repo — every layer and language (backend, frontend, scripts, tests, docs) — for both producers and consumers of the old shape.
  - Zero producers AND zero consumers found → delete it now, as part of the current change.
  - Still produced or consumed somewhere → it is not legacy, it is a live requirement (even if it's confusingly named or the comment calls it "backward compat"). Fix the name/comment instead of deleting the behavior — don't confuse "badly named" with "dead."
- **When the code alone can't prove it either way, ask — don't guess.** Some producers/consumers live outside the repo you can grep: an admin manually pasting AI-tool output, old bookmarked URLs, SEO backlinks, a third-party webhook, another service entirely. If you can't determine liveness from the codebase, stop and ask the user directly. Don't default to silently keeping it "to be safe," and don't default to silently deleting it either — both are guesses.
- **Don't manufacture optionality you can decide yourself.** Every new setting, flag, mode, or "supports both the old and new format" branch is a decision you're pushing onto a future reader/user/maintainer instead of making yourself now. Default to ONE deliberate path; only add a toggle when there's a proven, *current* need for both behaviors to coexist — never speculatively, "in case someone still needs the old one." If it doesn't serve a real, current need, cut it rather than let it linger as unused surface area.
- **A "kept for compatibility" comment is itself a code smell, not a shield.** If you encounter one while touching a file, verify it right then (grep for real usage) instead of carrying it forward unquestioned. Either the comment is right — then say concretely what still needs it — or it's stale, in which case remove the legacy path and the comment together.
- **Apply the Boy Scout Rule at the feature level, not just the line level.** When a file you're touching has a dual-format branch, a deprecated stub, or a "for older clients" fallback, take the extra step of checking whether the old side is provably unreachable — and if so, remove it as part of the same change rather than walking past it again next time.

## Naming Consistency: Stable → Volatile Ordering
- **Most-stable concept first, least-stable last, everywhere — in any language.** When a name is composed of multiple parts (filename, class, function, variable, table/column, JSON key), order the parts from the most invariant/general concept to the most specific/variable one — the same discipline as `YYYY-MM-DD` (year is more stable than day) or `last_name_first_name` (surname is the more stable grouping key). This is not about dates specifically — apply it to every compound name: `curriculum_node_id` not `id_curriculum_node`, `audit_run_status` not `status_audit_run`, `userEmailPending` not `pendingUserEmail` when "pending" is the volatile qualifier. Applies equally to a Python `user_email_pending`, a JS `userEmailPending`, or a PHP `$userEmailPending`.
- **Why it matters:** consistent stable-first ordering makes same-concept items sort and group together (alphabetically, in a directory listing, in autocomplete) instead of scattering based on which incidental qualifier happens to lead.
- **Test-file naming is a common place this breaks down** — pick ONE convention (e.g. subject-first, role-suffix: `audit_pipeline_test.php`, `parser_test.py`, `authForm.test.tsx`) and apply it to every new test file across every language in the repo; don't let PHP tests, JS tests, and Python tests each invent their own scheme, and don't mix prefix-style (`test_x`) and suffix-style (`x_test`) within the same language.
- **Make the entry point vs. sub-scripts distinction visible.** A directory mixing an orchestrator script (one that discovers and chains/runs every other script) with the scripts it orchestrates must make that hierarchy obvious from naming alone (a distinct prefix like `run_`/`_runner` that doesn't collide with the subject-first convention used by the things it runs) — or, better, move the sub-scripts into their own subdirectory so the entry point is the only file at that level.

## Writing Style: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) — Comments AND Prose
- **State the point first, justify it after.** Any comment longer than 2–3 lines should open with the actual conclusion/instruction/gotcha, then follow with the supporting reasoning, trade-offs, or incident history — never the reverse. Don't make the reader wade through a paragraph of backstory before learning what the comment is actually telling them. Applies to `//`, `#`, `"""docstrings"""`, `/** JSDoc */` alike.
- **No literal "BLUF:" label needed** — just structure the comment that way: lead with the rule/gotcha, then explain why it exists.
- **This is the default for ALL written text, not just code comments.** Chat responses, PR/commit descriptions, `README`/`docs/` prose, and explanations of a change all follow the same shape: lead with the answer/result/decision, then give supporting detail — never open with throat-clearing, process narration, or backstory before the point. If a longer explanation is needed, put it after the headline, not before it.

## Strong Typing & Explicit Visibility (per-language mechanisms)
The principle is universal — make types and access boundaries explicit so a reader (or the compiler/linter) can catch mistakes without tracing every call site. The mechanism differs by language; use whichever your file is written in:

- **PHP:** `declare(strict_types=1);` at the top of every new/edited file. Type every parameter, return type (including `?nullable`, union types, `void`/`never`), property, and class constant. Never leave a bare `$prop` — always `private string $prop;` etc.
- **TypeScript/JavaScript:** prefer TypeScript over plain JS where the project already uses it; keep `strict`/`noImplicitAny` on in `tsconfig.json`. Type every function parameter and return value explicitly rather than relying on inference across a public API boundary. Avoid `any` — use `unknown` + narrowing, a proper interface/type, or generics instead. For plain JS files, use JSDoc `@param`/`@returns` annotations as the equivalent of type signatures.
- **Python:** type-hint every function signature (`def f(x: int) -> str:`), including `Optional[...]`/`| None`. Use `dataclasses`/`TypedDict`/`pydantic` models instead of passing raw untyped `dict`s across module boundaries. Run/keep compatible with `mypy` (or the project's configured type checker) rather than relying on duck typing for anything but the most local, obvious cases.
- **Any other language:** apply the same intent — explicit parameter/return/property types wherever the language supports static or gradual typing, and a structured value type (record/struct/DTO) instead of an untyped generic map/dict/array when the same shape recurs (ties back to the DRY-concepts rule above: a shape used in 2+ places is a concept, not a coincidence).
- **Explicit visibility on every property, constant, and method — never rely on a language's implicit/default visibility.** Start from the most restrictive option (`private` in PHP/TS/Java-style languages; a leading underscore `_name` convention plus module-level encapsulation in Python; `#private` fields in modern JS classes), widen to `protected`/module-level only when a subclass or sibling module genuinely needs it, and to fully `public`/exported only for the actual external API. An unmarked/implicitly-public member forces every future reader to grep the entire codebase just to find out whether it's safe to change or remove — explicit restriction is itself documentation that "this is never used outside this unit," which is exactly the clarity we want (same spirit as the Liskov/Interface-Segregation note above: don't expose more than callers need).
- **When you encounter an existing member with no visibility marker, or a wider visibility/export than its actual usage requires**, narrow it as part of the Boy Scout Rule — but first grep for external usages (same discipline as the field-migration rule above), across every language that might call into it, so narrowing `public` → `private` (or removing an export) doesn't silently break a caller you didn't see.
- **Prefer strict/type-safe comparisons over loose/coercing ones — this is the same "make types explicit" principle applied to comparison operators, not a separate rule.** A loose comparison silently coerces mismatched types instead of surfacing the mismatch, which defeats the whole point of typing parameters and returns above.
  - **PHP:** use `===`/`!==`, never bare `==`/`!=` (classic footguns: `0 == 'abc'` is `true` pre-PHP 8, `'1e2' == '100'` is `true`). Use `in_array($x, $arr, true)`, `array_search($x, $arr, true)`, and `switch`/`match` with `match` preferred (it's strict-by-default) over `switch` (which compares loosely).
  - **JavaScript/TypeScript:** use `===`/`!==`, never `==`/`!=` (except the narrow, idiomatic `x == null` shorthand for "null or undefined", and only when that's genuinely the intent — prefer `x === null || x === undefined` when clarity matters more than brevity).
  - **Python:** use `==`/`!=` for value equality (Python has no loose/coercing equality operator, so this isn't a footgun the way it is in PHP/JS) but use `is`/`is not` for identity/`None` checks (`if x is None:`, never `if x == None:`).
  - **Any other language:** apply the same intent — pick whichever operator/construct in that language does NOT perform implicit type coercion, and use it by default; only reach for a coercing comparison when the coercion itself is the explicit, documented intent.
- **An unchecked numeric cast is the same footgun as a loose comparison — it just hides in the other direction.** `(int)$x` (PHP), `int(x)`/`Number(x)` (Python/JS), etc. on an unvalidated string silently maps `''`, `null`, `"abc"`, and other garbage to `0` — and if `0` (or any other cast-to default) happens to be a MEANINGFUL, valid value in your domain (a real enum member, a real "terminal/zero" state, a real id), the cast doesn't fail loudly, it silently produces a real, indistinguishable, WRONG value. This is worse than a loose `==` because there's no error to notice — the corrupted input just becomes valid-looking data. Before casting anything that didn't come from a schema/type-checked source (raw request input, a regex capture, a DB `JSON_EXTRACT`, an env var), validate the ORIGINAL string first with an ANCHORED full-string check, then only cast once validation passes; treat "didn't validate" as `null`/an explicit error, never as the cast's default.
  - **`is_numeric()` (PHP) — and its `float`/`Number.parseFloat`-based equivalents in other languages — is NOT sufficient validation on its own** for a domain that expects a plain integer token: it happily accepts scientific notation (`"0e123"`, `"1e2"`), leading `+`, hex-looking floats, and leading/trailing whitespace, all of which then `(int)`-cast to a value that looks like a valid, in-range answer (`(int)"0e123" === 0` — a real, meaningful rung/id/enum value in plenty of domains) instead of erroring. Prefer a closed-vocabulary membership check (e.g. `EvidenceLadderService::isRung()`) or an anchored `^-?\d+$`-style regex over `is_numeric()` whenever the accepted shape is "a plain integer," not "anything PHP's parser can coerce to a number."
  - **When an anchored regex captures an optional sign in its own group (to allow rejecting out-of-vocabulary negatives explicitly), the sign group MUST be recombined with the digits before casting/validating — never validate only the digit group and discard the sign.** E.g. `preg_match('/^(-?)(\d+)$/', $raw, $m)` then casting only `$m[2]` silently turns an invalid `"-65"` into a "valid-looking" `65`; use `(int)($m[1] . $m[2])` so the closed-vocabulary check (`isRung(-65)`) correctly rejects the actual, signed value instead of a truncated positive one.
- **A regex/parse that is meant to validate "is this whole token X" must be anchored to the WHOLE input, never just "contains X somewhere."** `preg_match('/\d+/', $raw, $m)` (or the equivalent `.search()`/unanchored regex in any language) matches the FIRST occurrence anywhere in the string — so `$raw = "[T65 | T48 | ...]"` (a model echoing an option list back verbatim) parses as `65`, a plausible-looking but entirely wrong answer, instead of being rejected. Use `^...$` (or the language's full-match equivalent, e.g. Python's `re.fullmatch`) whenever the intent is "the whole field IS this shape," and reserve unanchored matching for genuine substring-search use cases.


## Self-Improving Process: This File Is Fed By Review Feedback
- **When a code review (human or automated) flags a bug pattern this document didn't already warn against, update THIS file in the same change that fixes the bug** — not as a separate, optional follow-up. The fix closes one instance; the instructions-update is what stops the SAME class of mistake from being suggested again next time. A review comment that reveals a gap in these instructions is itself a piece of feedback about the instructions, not just about the code.
- **Generalize the fix into a principle, don't just log the incident.** Don't transcribe "line 87 had a bug" — extract the reusable rule the specific bug was an instance of (e.g. "an unchecked numeric cast silently maps invalid input to a valid-looking default"), state it once, and let it apply to every future occurrence of that shape, in any language, anywhere in the repo — same spirit as the DRY-concepts rules above, applied to the instructions file itself.
- **Prefer strengthening or extending an existing bullet over bolting on a near-duplicate one.** Before adding a new rule, check whether an existing rule already covers the principle and just needs a sharper example, an extra sentence, or a cross-reference — a bloated, redundant instructions file is exactly the kind of drift this document tells you to prune elsewhere (see Legacy Code & Feature Rot above).
- **Treat this as a standing habit, not a one-off ask.** Any time you (the assistant) receive explicit feedback on the quality or correctness of a suggestion — via a code review comment, a user correction, or a rejected suggestion — pause and ask: "does `.github/copilot-instructions.md` already prevent this, and if not, should it?" If the answer is no and the pattern is likely to recur, propose the addition without waiting to be asked.
